howto.name: How to check AI prior authorization in a marketplace plan for compliance

steps.name: Register every tool in the authorization path
steps.text: List each algorithm or AI system that scores, routes or decides prior authorization requests for marketplace members, with the criteria it applies and the decisions it feeds.

steps.name: Prove clinician review of denials
steps.text: For every medical necessity denial, show the licensed clinician who reviewed it and the record they saw, with the tool's output as one input.

steps.name: Measure the clocks and publish the metrics
steps.text: Report urgent decisions against 72 hours and standard decisions against 7 days, and publish the annual counts of requests, approvals, denials, overturns and decision times that CMS-0057-F requires.

steps.name: Put a specific reason on every denial
steps.text: Audit denial notices for a clinically grounded reason and clear appeal instructions; a vague automated rejection is now a rule violation, not a style problem.

steps.name: Run the Section 1557 review
steps.text: Identify decision support tools that use race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability as inputs, document the mitigation, and keep the record OCR would ask for.

short: How AI is used in Affordable Care Act marketplace plans' prior authorization and clinical decisions, the CMS-0057-F rule in force since January 2026, the insurer pledge, Section 1557, and how to appeal.
title: ACA Marketplace Plans and AI
subtitle: Prior authorization, the 2026 federal rule and a consumer's rights
body_html:
On this page

  • Who this page is for
  • Where AI touches marketplace coverage
  • The federal rule: CMS-0057-F
  • The industry pledge, and how it is going
  • Section 1557 and decision support tools
  • What a marketplace consumer can do
  • What insurers and providers must show
  • Sources

Who this page is for

A person with an Affordable Care Act marketplace plan who wants to know whether software is deciding what the plan will approve, and what their rights are when it says no. And an insurer, a plan vendor or a provider that uses artificial intelligence in prior authorization or clinical decisions for marketplace members. The federal rules that govern this arrived in January 2026 and reach further than most consumers know. This page covers the individual and family plans sold through HealthCare.gov and the state marketplaces; Medicare is on the Medicare and AI page.

Where AI touches marketplace coverage

Prior authorization. Marketplace insurers, like every other line of business, now use software and AI to compare a request against coverage rules and clinical criteria, often in seconds. Physicians report that some of these tools raise denial rates by scoring the request against averages rather than the patient in front of them. The American Medical Association's 2025 physician survey found practices completing about 40 prior authorizations a week, with 32 percent of physicians saying requests are often or always denied.

Clinical decision support. Providers who take marketplace coverage use AI in triage, imaging, risk scoring and documentation. Those tools fall under the Section 1557 rule below whatever the patient's coverage.

Coding and cost. AI documentation tools such as ambient scribes capture more of each visit, which raises coded intensity and, insurer groups argue, premiums. That is a cost pressure on the individual market rather than a coverage decision, but it is where much of the money in this subject moves.

The federal rule: CMS-0057-F

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F, January 2024) applies to qualified health plan issuers on the federally facilitated marketplaces, alongside Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and CHIP managed care. Its operational requirements took effect January 1, 2026:

  • Decision clocks. Urgent requests must be decided within 72 hours and standard requests within 7 calendar days.
  • A specific reason for every denial. A denied request must carry a specific reason, which ends the vague automated rejection and gives the member and the provider something to appeal against.
  • Public reporting. Plans must publish prior authorization metrics each year: how many requests, how many approved, denied and overturned on appeal, and how long decisions took.
  • Electronic exchange. By January 1, 2027, plans must offer standard FHIR interfaces so requests, decisions and reasons move between provider and plan systems electronically.

The rule does not ban AI in these decisions, and it does not itself require a clinician to review a denial. Those obligations come from state insurance law, from Medicare Advantage rules for that program, and from the voluntary pledge below. State-based marketplaces that are not federally facilitated are outside CMS-0057-F, though most state insurance codes impose their own prior authorization timelines.

The industry pledge, and how it is going

On June 23, 2025, more than 50 insurers signed a set of six voluntary commitments through AHIP, covering commercial, marketplace, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans for roughly 250 million people:

  • Every denial based on medical necessity is reviewed by a licensed, qualified clinician. Stated as already in effect.
  • A member who changes plans during a course of treatment has the previous plan's authorization honored for 90 days, for the same in-network benefit. From January 1, 2026.
  • Fewer services subject to prior authorization, with reductions from January 1, 2026.
  • Clear explanations of decisions and of how to appeal, for fully insured and commercial coverage from January 1, 2026.
  • Standard electronic prior authorization on FHIR interfaces across all lines of business by January 1, 2027.
  • At least 80 percent of electronic approvals answered in real time in 2027.

The pledge carries no enforcement; the federal rule does. In April 2026, AHIP and the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association reported that participating plans had removed 6.5 million prior authorizations, about 11 percent. The AMA's 2025 survey, released in May 2026, found only 24 percent of physicians saying denials are consistently reviewed by an appropriately qualified clinician, which is the one commitment that was supposed to apply from day one.

Section 1557 and decision support tools

Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act prohibits discrimination in health programs that receive federal money, which includes marketplace insurers and the providers who accept their coverage. The May 2024 HHS rule added 45 CFR 92.210, in force since May 1, 2025: a covered entity must not discriminate through a patient care decision support tool, must make reasonable efforts to identify tools that use race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability as an input, and must make reasonable efforts to mitigate the risk of discrimination from them. The term covers AI models, clinical algorithms, flowcharts and predictive analytics alike. HHS's Office for Civil Rights investigates complaints and can require corrective action; the site's HHS OCR AI enforcement page covers the process and the evidence OCR expects.

For a provider this means three practical duties: know which of your tools use protected characteristics as inputs (a vendor questionnaire is the usual first step), document the steps taken to reduce the risk, and keep the clinician's independent judgment in the record, since an AI recommendation is not a defence to a discriminatory decision.

What a marketplace consumer can do

If a service is denied. Every marketplace plan must offer an internal appeal and, if that fails, an external review by an independent reviewer whose decision binds the plan (45 CFR 147.136). You generally have 180 days from the denial to start the internal appeal. An urgent case must be decided within 72 hours, and you may ask for expedited external review at the same time. The denial notice must tell you the specific reason and how to appeal; if it does not, that is itself a complaint to your state insurance department.

Ask what decided it. You are entitled to the clinical criteria the plan applied and to know whether a qualified clinician reviewed a medical necessity denial. Ask your doctor to write to the individual facts of your case, because that is what an average-based tool leaves out.

If you are changing plans during treatment. Ask the new plan to honor the existing authorization for 90 days under the industry commitment, and check whether your state requires it by law.

Where to complain. Your state insurance department for coverage decisions; HHS Office for Civil Rights for discrimination; the marketplace call center for enrollment. Nothing on this page is legal or medical advice; for your own case, use the primary sources below and your plan's own notices.

What insurers and providers must show

For an insurer: a register of every algorithm and AI tool in the prior authorization path and what it decides; evidence that medical necessity denials are reviewed by a qualified clinician with the tool's output as one input; decision time reporting against the 72 hour and 7 day clocks and the public metrics CMS-0057-F requires; specific, clinically grounded denial reasons on every notice; and the FHIR interfaces due in 2027. For a provider: the Section 1557 tool inventory and mitigation record, and documentation that the clinician, not the tool, made the decision. The site's HIPAA and AI page covers the privacy side, which applies to both.

Sources

  • CMS, Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, CMS-0057-F, 89 FR 8758, February 8, 2024.
  • AHIP, Improving Prior Authorization for Patients and Providers, commitments announced June 23, 2025; AHIP and BCBSA progress report, April 2026.
  • American Medical Association, 2025 Prior Authorization Physician Survey, released May 2026.
  • HHS, Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities, Section 1557 final rule, May 2024, 45 CFR 92.210.
  • 45 CFR 147.136, internal claims and appeals and external review processes.
